guide.text:
Week 44 / The bag that copies / Adult guide
The bag that copies
Mathematics before the session
Start with one red and one blue counter. At each step choose uniformly among the counters now
present, return the chosen counter, and add one new counter of its color. After n draws the bag has
n+2 counters. If r of the draws were red, its composition is (r+1) red and (n-r+1) blue. Every r from 0
through n is possible, and neither color can disappear.
This is the one-copy Pólya urn. At every fixed length n, the number of red draws is uniform on
0,1,...,n: each total has probability 1/(n+1). This does not say that color words are equally likely. A
particular length-n word with r reds has probability r!(n-r)!/(n+1)!, independent of their order. There
are n!/[r!(n-r)!] such words, giving the stated uniform total.
Counter identities make a finite proof visible. At successive draws there are 2, 3, ..., n+1 identities
available. A history specifies the particular counter drawn each time, with new copies labeled by their
birth step. All (n+1)! such histories are equally likely, although the available identities depend on the
earlier draws. For n=2 there are six histories, with two histories each for zero, one, or two red draws.
For n=3 there are 24 histories, six per total.
The important distinctions
A color word such as RR merges two two-draw identity histories; RB has only one. Thus the four words
RR, RB, BR, BB have probabilities 1/3, 1/6, 1/6, 1/3. If instead the original RB bag is restored after
every draw and no copy is added, those four color words each have probability 1/4, and the red-draw
totals have probabilities 1/4, 1/2, 1/4.
The copying draws are dependent: after red, the next red chance is 2/3; after blue, it is 1/3. Yet
reordering a word without changing its color totals does not change its probability. This
exchangeability follows from multiplying the same red factors 1 through r and blue factors 1 through
n-r over the same denominators 2 through n+1. Do not confuse it with independence.
All probability claims assume uniform selection of current identities at each step and the stated initial
bag and addition rule. Deliberately choosing a legal word proves possibility, not its probability. Trial
frequencies can inspire the equal-total conjecture but do not prove it. No claim about eventual loss of
a color follows; both original counters remain at every finite time.
What each group is discovering
K-1: changes of composition, multiple stories with the same finish, and working backward one draw.
Grades 2-3: color stories versus equally likely marked histories, and the contrast with return-only
sampling. Grades 4-5: exact total distributions, equal-count reordering, and a general conjecture
supported by a finite counting proof.
Bellingham Math Circle / Prepared October 2026 / Unpiloted
1

Week 44 / The bag that copies / Adult guide
Running the session
Materials and readiness
For eleven children, prepare six opaque bags/cups and, per pair, six red plus six blue counters of
equal size and feel. Only one of each begins inside. Keep the supply outside. Use removable identity
labels: original counters R1 and B1; the first new copy is R2 or B2; the next is R3 or B3. The digit
records when the copy was added, not the number of that color. A marker and small paper slips
suffice.
Print K-1 pages 1-4, grades 2-3 pages 1-5 and grades 4-5 pages 1-4, and supply pencils plus a small
tray for each ending bag. K-1 requires counting to six, color matching, and an adult reading the
questions. Middle work requires tracking two draws and distinguishing identities. Upper work uses
branching counts and small products; factorial notation is optional. Have an adult enact the first
copied draw and supervise resetting to exactly R1/B1 before every fresh story. Prepared, unpiloted
material.
Short shared launch
Let the group inspect RB. Deliberately take R out, visibly put that same R back, and add a second red:
RB → draw R → RRB. Write the story in a strip as you go, one color per cell. Do a second draw so
children see that both red identities can be selected. Ask, “What bags could be here after two draws?”
Announce when children are choosing a possible story and when a cup is being used for a random
draw.
A flexible hour
0-5 minutes: running around. 5-10: handle counters and demonstrate returning plus copying.
10-22: choose short stories and compare final bags; the random games on page 6 add about 15
minutes. 22-33: K-1 extends or reverses stories; older groups construct the six marked two-draw
histories. 33-35: movement break: one child is the original counter, another joins as its copy. 35-47:
compare return-only sampling or investigate three/four draws. 47-53: share an exact count or an
invariant with the group. 53-56: restore the starting kits.
A complete six-history argument is a strong endpoint. Do not insist that K-1 compute probabilities or
that the oldest children enumerate 120 rows. Let the upper group use the 24-history result to predict
the next stage. An unexplained five-draw guess should be recorded as a conjecture until justified.
Optional hints
For final bags: “How many reds were added?” For the marked tree: “After the first draw, point to each
counter that could be chosen next.” For reordered words: “Which multipliers change, and which only
move?” For backward work: “Which one counter could have been the last new copy?”
Source and adaptation
Janko Gravner, UC Davis MAT 235B, Martingale convergence theorems, February 2, 2024, slides 12-14, “Pólya’s
urn”; university lecture PDF. The source gives the urn and uniform count law. Marked-counter histories, short-story
tasks, and the exact finite keys here are independently derived classroom adaptations; no martingale theorem is a
child prerequisite.
Bellingham Math Circle / Prepared October 2026 / Unpiloted

K to 1 answer key
Problem 1
After two draws the possible bags are 3R/1B from RR, 2R/2B from RB or BR, and 1R/3B from BB.
Only the middle bag has two different two-draw color stories. A child who counts marked counters
instead finds two stories for every bag (R1 R1 or R1 R2; R1 B1 or B1 R1; B1 B1 or B1 B2): accept that,
then ask which bags have two different color orders. This is a possibility question; counting these four
words as equally likely would be wrong for random copying.
Problem 2
For the printed choices: 4R/1B is possible via RRR; 2R/3B via RBB, BRB, or BBR; 5R/0B is impossible;
1R/4B via BBB. The full collection of possible three-draw bags also includes 3R/2B, via RRB, RBR, or
BRR: ask for it as a follow-up. The all-red picture is impossible because the original blue is never
removed.
Problem 3
The displayed 3R/3B finish requires exactly two red draws and two blue draws. All six color stories are
RRBB, RBRB, RBBR, BRRB, BRBR, BBRR. The page has eight story rows, two more than needed.
Completeness can be seen by choosing the two red positions among four: (1,2), (1,3), (1,4), (2,3),
(2,4), (3,4).
The four-draw bags with more blue than red are exactly 1R/5B, made by BBBB, and 2R/4B, made by
RBBB, BRBB, BBRB, or BBBR. The bag has six counters, with at least one of each color; the other
mixtures are tied or red-majority. The two bag boxes, each with a story row, hold these. Children need
a story for each blue-majority bag, not necessarily all four stories for the second bag.

All three compositions have two histories, so none has the most: each has probability 1/3. Notice that

Problem 3
Copying: zero, one, two red draws are tied at 2/6 = 1/3 each. Return only: RR, RB, BR, BB are now
four equally likely histories, so the totals have weights 1, 2, 1 and probabilities 1/4, 1/2, 1/4. One red
draw is most likely in the unchanged bag. Copying increases the chance of repeating the first color.
Problem 4
The stories are RRB, RBR, BRR. Each has chance 1/12: RRB gives (1/2)(2/3)(1/4); RBR gives
(1/2)(1/3)(2/4); BRR gives (1/2)(1/3)(2/4). Each represents two of the 24 marked histories.
Problem 5
5R/1B: only RRRR, because all four added counters must be red. 4R/2B: four stories, RRRB, RRBR,
RBRR, BRRR. 3R/3B: six stories, RRBB, RBRB, RBBR, BRRB, BRBR, BBRR, one for each choice of the
two red draws.
Problem 6
Neither: each has chance 1/5. RRRR has 1 × 2 × 3 × 4 = 24 of the 120 marked histories, since its red
draws have 1, 2, 3 and 4 red counters to choose from. Each of the six 3R/3B color stories has 1 × 2 ×
1 × 2 = 4, so that bag also has 24. An adult can carry the multiplication.

Week 44 / The bag that copies / Adult guide
Grades 4 to 5 answer key
Problem 1
The six marked histories are (R1,R1), (R1,R2), (R1,B1), (B1,R1), (B1,B1), (B1,B2). Each has probability
1/6. The first two have two red draws, the middle two have one, and the last two have zero. All totals
are tied, two histories each.
Problem 2
Without copies, the four histories are RR, RB, BR, BB, each with probability 1/4. The probabilities for
zero, one, two reds become 1/4, 1/2, 1/4, compared with 1/3, 1/3, 1/3 under copying. In copying, the
first color gains an extra identity for the second draw, giving RR and BB two marked histories each.
Problem 3
RRB, RBR, BRR each has probability 1/12. Their products are (1/2)(2/3)(1/4), (1/2)(1/3)(2/4), and
(1/2)(1/3)(2/4). Reordering does not change the product of the red factors and blue factors. The draws
remain dependent despite this equality.
Problem 4
There are six marked histories for each total 0, 1, 2, 3. BBB and RRR each have 1 × 2 × 3 = 6 identity
histories. For one red, the three words RBB, BRB, BBR have two histories each, hence six. The three
words with two reds also have two each. These four groups cover all eight possible color words and all
24 marked histories.
Problem 5

in each three-draw group by the five available fourth-draw identities. The contributions to totals 0

Problem 6
Predict 1/6 for each red total after five draws, and 1/(n+1) after n draws. Proof: a word with r reds has
probability r!(n-r)!/(n+1)!, since its red numerators are 1,...,r and its blue numerators 1,...,n-r. There
are n!/[r!(n-r)!] such words. Multiplication gives 1/(n+1). A child’s observed pattern remains a
conjecture until justified; the general proof is an optional endpoint invited by the problem.

Starting routes and return visits
Planning update of 4 October 2026. The timing menus are examples; a theme can continue over several meetings. Keep the full
Grades 4-5 investigations and choose by readiness.
Use and return choices
Keep one adult at each table and reset every fresh story to the same two original counters. First routes:
K-1 P1-2; grades 2-3 P1-2; grades 4-5 P1, then P2-3. Before the first chance question (grades 2-3 P2,
grades 4-5 P1), pairs draw without looking for about ten two-draw copying games, then about ten

games take about 15 minutes. A chart of 20 pooled games of each kind shows fewer two-red, two-blue
bags for copying than for returning only about four times in five, so a chart that does not is ordinary
chance; the exact count decides. On return, K-1 can find four-draw stories or work backward one step
(P3-4). Grades 2-3 can compare return-only sampling and reordered words (P3-4), then larger final bags
(P5-6). Grades 4-5 can make the 24-history argument (P4), the four-draw count (P5), or pursue the
arbitrary-length conjecture (P6). Keep exact history counts distinct from trial frequencies.

bonus-guide.text:
Week 44 / The bag that copies / Bonus facilitator
Bellingham Math Circle / Week 44 / W44-BONUS-FAC-v4 / Unpiloted
1
Mathematical overview
Start R1,B1 and choose uniformly among current counter identities, returning every draw. In the usual
copying rule, two red-draw totals 0,1,2 have probabilities 2/6,2/6,2/6. If each returned draw instead
adds one counter of the OTHER color, those totals have probabilities 1/6,4/6,1/6. With no addition they
have probabilities 1/4,2/4,1/4. In this two-draw comparison, opposite reinforcement promotes
switching and balanced draw totals; copying promotes repeating. No general balance law follows from
this one comparison. The six add-a-counter histories each have probability (1/2)(1/3), while the four
no-add histories each have (1/2)(1/2). Equal histories must be compared within their own mechanism,
then via ratios; the different raw denominators cannot be ignored.
Under copying, after a history with r red draws and b blue draws, the current bag is (r+1)R,(b+1)B.
The next red chance is (r+1)/(r+b+2), not the original 1/2. The order does not affect this forecast
because the count bag is the same. After four draws the red chance is 1/6,2/6,3/6,4/6 or 5/6. Extremal
design is attainable by BBBB or RRRR; a tied forecast requires two of each color. Different orders with
the same totals give the same next-draw prediction. This is dependence across draws, not evidence
for independent trials with a fixed p.
Start one counter of each of three colors and copy the drawn color. After n draws the added-count
vector (r,b,g) ranges over all nonnegative triples summing to n. Each vector has chance 1/C(n+2,2).
Each particular word has probability 2r!b!g!/(n+2)!, so words need not be equally likely. There are
(n+2)!/2 equal marked-identity histories and n! histories per vector. For n=2: twelve histories, six
vectors, two each. For n=3: sixty histories, ten vectors, six each. The final bag counts are
(r+1,b+1,g+1); original colors never vanish. The theorem assumes one initial counter per color, one
same-color addition per returned draw and uniform identity selection. Other initial bags or feedback
rules can give different laws.
Grades 2-3 can compare short feedback rules and make concrete next-draw bags. Grades 4-5 can sort
three-color histories, explain equal vector weights and extend the count law. K-1 can enact the
opposite-color addition and build strongest/weakest/tied bags with adult reading and counting to six;
the complete marked probability comparison remains a readiness-dependent continuation.
Experiments produce conjectures; exact marked histories and count-product arguments establish the
chance claims.
Materials, route, and flexible time
Per pair: one opaque bag/cup, six red, six blue and six green same-size/same-feel counters, a tray for
the outside supply, removable labels 1-5, pencil and three student pages. Only the stated originals
start inside; reset before every new story. Labels name color plus birth step, as in the base packet:
original R1/B1/G1; the first new copy is R2, B2 or G2 depending on its color, the next is 3. They do not
number same-color counters consecutively. A second page-3 print can be cut into the twelve supplied
movable history cards by an adult; children may write the final color counts on those cards and
pool/sort them. Cutting stays in preparation, not a child task. For the three-draw return, add ten blank
100-by-60 mm count-record cards with three columns labeled R, B, G, thirty blank 70-by-25 mm
history slips, and two blank Letter sheets per pair. These are paper records rather than physical
counter-fit mats: children retain one card for each final count bag and place supporting words/count
evidence beneath it. If choosing full identity enumeration rather than color-word weights, supply thirty
further slips on that return visit. There is no exact-size board fit claim.
For eleven children at K–1 / 2–3 / 4–5: five kits, five bags/trays, thirty counters of each color (90 total),
five label sets and pencils, fifty count-record cards, 150 blank history slips and ten blank Letter sheets
(150 further slips only if all five kits choose full three-draw identity enumeration). The upper third child
rotates as banker/checker. Print five shared companions and five extra copies of page 3 for movable
cards, or eleven selected recording pages as desired. Three anchored adults supervise the addition
rule and resets while children choose stories, construct bags and compare forecasts. A partner
handles the outside supply and checks each returned counter plus exactly one legal addition.
Shared launch, 4-6 minutes: let children handle R/B. Demonstrate the non-target single
opposite-reinforcement step R1,B1 -> draw R1 -> return R1 and add B2 -> R1,B1,B2, as pictured. Let

Bellingham Math Circle / Week 44 / W44-BONUS-FAC-v4 / Unpiloted

a child select a legal next identity. Explicitly restore originals before changing rules. Before Problem 3,
demonstrate G1 returning and adding G2 in R1,B1,G1; the next draw can now choose G2. Distinguish
deliberately chosen possible stories from hidden random draws.
A manageable first visit can spend 15-25 minutes comparing two rules, then 15-20 on forecasts. Add
the no-add comparison only after children know which bag the second draw uses. Three-color copying
can be a separate 20-35 minute visit. Pooled twelve-card sorting is enough before extending to sixty
histories; no one should transcribe a sixty-row table. Before a three-draw return, place the ten blank
count cards and history slips in the kit. Let children choose predicted count bags and retain them on
separate cards, then attach exact evidence; cards with the same final R/B/G counts can be merged.
Children may extend the twelve printed two-draw cards by listing the five possible third identities,
pooling first-draw groups and using one recoverable story per slip. Alternatively, retain each distinct
color word on one of 27 slips, use actual available same-color choices to find its identity multiplicity,
and attach that weight to its final-bag card. A child need not duplicate either complete collection. Do
not silently operate the whole investigation for them: offer a choice of these record routes only when
needed. The oldest children may use count-group transitions or a reversible count argument instead.
Finishing every page is unnecessary.
Problem 1 (page 1)
For copying the complete identity histories are (R1,R1),(R1,R2),(R1,B1),(B1,R1),(B1,B1),(B1,B2). The
middle two give one red and one blue draw, hence 2/6=1/3.
For opposite reinforcement: (R1,R1) has two red draws; (R1,B1),(R1,B2),(B1,R1),(B1,R2) have one red;
(B1,B1) has zero red. These six are equally likely. The no-add column has two spare lines; the six
printed lines in a column do not assert six legal histories under every rule. Thus one of each has
chance 4/6=2/3, greatest among the three rules. Note that added counter B2 exists after R1, and
added R2 exists after B1. The complete no-add stories are RR,RB,BR,BB, all equally likely, giving one
of each in 2/4=1/2. Fractions can be compared using six and four equally weighted models or an
adult-supported common denominator; raw successes 4,2,2 alone are not a chance proof.
With opposite reinforcement final bags and draw totals reverse the usual copying correspondence: RR
ends 1R/3B, RB/BR end 2R/2B, BB ends 3R/1B. All original colors persist under every rule. Hints: after
the first R, inspect which identities are available next; keep the two additions visibly different.
Extension: compare three draws and ask whether the opposite rule always favors the most balanced
totals; do not claim a general law from two draws.
New versus base: base middle/upper Problem 3/2 compares copying with no additions. The new
mechanism is opposite-color reinforcement and its balance-promoting distribution. The familiar two
controls support the new comparison and are not separately counted as investigations.
Problem 2 (page 2)
Strongest red: RRRR, final 5R/1B, next red 5/6. Weakest red: BBBB, final 1R/5B, next red 1/6. Tied: any
of RRBB,RBRB,RBBR,BRRB,BRBR,BBRR, final 3R/3B, next red 1/2. None can forecast certainty because
both original colors persist.
Other attainable forecasts are 4R/2B (2/3) and 2R/4B (1/3). For example RRRB and RRBR give the first,
RBBB and BRBB the second. The extreme forecast has only one four-draw color story; every
intermediate forecast has multiple orders. Children may give “five of the six counters” rather than
symbolic fractions. A live partner bet can test the executable forecast but cannot establish its exact
probability through a small sample.
Hint: put the current counters in a visible row and ask how many would win the next red bet.
Extension: after a red next draw, update a formerly tied bag and its forecast; show that later evidence
changes the prediction again. These are continuations within the forecasting investigation.
New versus base: the base enumerates finishing bags and equal-count story chances. This reverses
the direction to design a predictive bag and forecast the NEXT random draw conditional on the current
state, with extremal and tied targets.

Problem 3 (page 3)
The twelve printed stories are all original identities available after the first draw plus that draw's one
new copy. Each has probability 1/(3×4). The six final bags, in R/B/G order, are
(3,1,1),(1,3,1),(1,1,3),(2,2,1),(2,1,2),(1,2,2). Each gets two identity histories. A repeated word such as
RR has two histories (R1,R1),(R1,R2); a mixed word RG has one, but its reversed word GR adds the
second history to the same final bag.
After three draws, added vectors are permutations of (3,0,0), of (2,1,0), and (1,1,1): three plus six plus
one = ten. Their final counts add one to every coordinate. Each vector has six of the sixty marked
histories. For (3,0,0), the one color word has 1×2×3=6 identity histories; for a (2,1,0) vector, three
word orders each have 2!=2 histories; for (1,1,1), six distinct orders each have one history. Those
three types cover all nonnegative triples summing to three.
General adult explanation: for fixed vector (r,b,g), each color word has the same product r!b!g! of
available-color choices. There are n!/(r!b!g!) words, so multiplying gives n! marked histories per
vector. Total histories are 3×4×...×(n+2)=(n+2)!/2, yielding 1/C(n+2,2). Children can work with
paired rearrangements and grouped small cases; factorial notation is not required.
Hints: ignore identity labels only AFTER reconstructing the final bag; keep a counter of each original
color in the tray record. Extension: arrange the vectors as points in a triangular count board; ask what
neighboring points mean when one added color is changed. This is an optional next representation,
not required alongside concurrent draw tallies.
New versus base: the base proves the binary total law, including arbitrary n. Three colors introduce a
two-dimensional count vector, triangular number of states and equal weight across count bags
despite unequal ordered-word weights.
